1.4 — Movement I: Input, Direction, Vector

In video games, movement looks natural and effortless. In computer science it is an algorithm, built by breaking one complex behaviour into three smaller problems: read the player's input → calculate a motion vector → translate the position. Today you read Unity's input functions and write the foundational movement code for this entire game from scratch.

Where you are starting from. Open Assets/Scripts/PlayerController.cs. It is an empty shell — a class with two blank methods. Your character has a Transform and nothing else: no physics body, no collider. Everything your character does from here on, you write. That is the whole design of this course.
Read the Docs ~15 min

Before writing code, computer scientists read the documentation for the tools the engine already provides. Unity gives us several different ways to detect when a player touches the keyboard. Compare them:

Unity APIReturnsBehaviour
Input.GetAxis("Horizontal") float (−1.0 to 1.0) Smooth ramp. Gradually accelerates toward −1 or +1, then coasts back to 0 when you let go.
Input.GetAxisRaw("Horizontal") float (−1, 0, or 1) Instant snap. Returns exactly −1, 0 or 1 the moment a key changes, with no smoothing filter.
Input.GetKey(KeyCode.D) bool Binary state. True while the physical D key is held down; false otherwise.
transform.Translate(vector) void Offsets the position by a vector. A relative step: "move this far from wherever I am right now."

Notice that "Horizontal" and "Vertical" are quoted strings, not key names. They are virtual axes, defined in Edit → Project Settings → Input Manager. Open that window and read what each axis is actually bound to — you may be surprised how much is already wired up for you.

Socratic: Evaluating Multiple Ways to Solve a Problem

  1. If you were building a driving game, or a character with heavy momentum, which would give the better feel — GetAxis or GetAxisRaw? Why?
  2. If you were building a precision grid-based puzzle game, or a fast arcade game where you must stop on a dime, why might GetAxisRaw be the better choice?
  3. What happens if a player wants to use the arrow keys, or a USB game controller, instead of WASD? Why is asking for the virtual axis "Horizontal" more flexible than hardcoding KeyCode.D?
  4. You will use one of these today. Which one, and what does your choice cost you?
Read Function-Level Examples ~15 min

Do not look for a complete movement script to copy. In real software engineering you read how individual functions behave in isolation, understand their inputs and outputs, and then assemble them into your own architecture. Here are three isolated snippets, each from a completely different machine:

Example 1 — Polling an axis on a warehouse forklift:

// Reads virtual axis data (-1.0 to +1.0) from the driver's keys or joystick tilt
float steeringIntent = Input.GetAxis("Horizontal");

Example 2 — Constructing a vector for a freight elevator:

// A 2D vector with no horizontal motion, and a frame-scaled vertical displacement
Vector2 verticalStep = new Vector2(0, liftSpeed * Time.deltaTime);

Example 3 — Translating space on an airport conveyor belt:

// Directly offsets the Transform's coordinates by the supplied vector
transform.Translate(beltDisplacementVector);

Predict Before Building

  1. In Example 2, why is the first value 0? What would happen to the elevator if it also had a non-zero horizontal value?
  2. If liftSpeed is 4.0, how far does the elevator travel over one second of accumulated frames? What does Time.deltaTime have to do with your answer?
  3. Example 3 gives Translate a vector called a displacement. Displacement from what, exactly — and how is that different from a position?
Build Lab: Your Turn ~25 min

Your engineering mission: build two-axis movement in PlayerController.cs. You will construct the whole pipeline yourself by solving three modular sub-problems. Work in Assets/Scripts/PlayerController.cs — the class is already there, and already attached to the Player prefab.

Architectural specification for PlayerController.cs:

Variables & tuning knobs:

  • How do you expose a speed knob to the Inspector while keeping the field private? What data type should a speed be, and why does the f suffix matter in C#?
  • Do horizontal and vertical movement want separate speed knobs, or one shared speed? There is no single right answer — decide, and be ready to justify it.
  • What variables will hold the raw directional input you read from the keyboard?
  • What data type should hold a calculated displacement before you apply it — Vector2 or Vector3? Investigate what transform.Translate accepts, and whether a Vector2 can be handed to it.

Sub-problem 1 — read the input:

  • Which lifecycle method runs continuously, every frame, so it can capture input as it happens?
  • What are the exact names of Unity's two default movement axes? (You read them in the Input Manager — spelling counts, because a misspelled axis name throws an error rather than failing quietly.)
  • Where do you store those decimal values, which range from −1.0 to +1.0?

Sub-problem 2 — construct the vectors:

  • How do you instantiate a 2-dimensional vector in C#?
  • Why multiply the directional input by a speed and by Time.deltaTime? Think about what happens on a 240 Hz monitor versus a 60 Hz one if you leave Time.deltaTime out.
  • For horizontal movement, which vector component receives the calculated displacement, and which stays 0? What about vertical movement? Sketch both vectors on paper before you type them.

Sub-problem 3 — apply the translation:

  • Which built-in Transform method offsets a GameObject's position in world space?
  • You have two displacement vectors — one horizontal, one vertical. Do you pass them in one call or two, and what would the difference be?

Save your script, return to Unity, press Play, and press WASD or the arrow keys. Your character should now glide in all four directions.

Bug Hunt: Testing Assumptions

  1. Delete * Time.deltaTime from your vector calculation. What happens when you tap a direction key? Why does the character cross the entire map in a single frame?
  2. In the Inspector for the Player, set your horizontal speed knob to 0. What happens when you press A and D, versus W and S?
  3. Swap your two vectors — pass the vertical one where the horizontal belongs, and vice versa. Describe exactly what the character does now, and explain why.
  4. Now the interesting one. Walk your character straight into a wall and keep going. What happens? Look back at the component list from 1.2 — what does the Player not have that would be needed to stop it?
Keep that last answer. Walking through walls is not a mistake in your code — transform.Translate moves your character by editing coordinates directly, so it never asks the physics engine anything. It will happily put you inside a wall, because nothing ever told it not to. Whether that matters depends entirely on the game you are making. In the next lesson you will compare every way Unity offers to move an object, and decide which one this game actually needs.
Tinker ~10 min

Tinker: Comparing input functions live

  1. Replace Input.GetAxis("Horizontal") with Input.GetAxisRaw("Horizontal"). Run the game. How does stopping feel compared to before? Which one suits this game?
  2. Press W and D together to move diagonally. Does diagonal movement feel faster than moving in a straight line? (Hint: in 2D maths, what is the length of the hypotenuse of a right triangle with sides 1 and 1? What length do you actually want?)
  3. Set your two speed knobs to different values and move around. In top-down 2D games, why might a designer deliberately make vertical movement slightly slower than horizontal?

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • State the three sub-problems of character movement: input → vector → translation
  • Explain the difference between Input.GetAxis, Input.GetAxisRaw, and Input.GetKey
  • Explain why multiplying by Time.deltaTime is necessary
  • Find and tune your speed knobs in the Inspector while the game runs
  • Explain why your character can walk through a wall right now
  • Commit and push your new movement code to your GitHub fork
